mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullNew:
Identify who originally owed the duty, what performance was promised, and whether the obligee has an important interest in that particular person’s performance. Personal skill, trust, contractual restrictions, and the governing law may matter. Delegation does not discharge the delegating party: unless the obligee agrees otherwise, the original obligor remains liable even if the delegate has promised to perform (§ 318(3); UCC § 2-210(1)), and the obligee's agreement to a substitution produces a novation. A money debt is the standard delegable duty; a performance that depends on who performs is not, so an airport could refuse a substitute singer for Pavarotti though not a substitute tenant's rent (Metropolitan Airports Comm'n, C&M 1216).

mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullNew:
Lawrence concerns a promise to pay another person’s debt. Seaver concerns a promise to provide for someone in a will. Those cases explore why the person benefited may sue despite not making the bargain. The two Sisney cases involve distinct arrangements and different evidence about an intention to create enforceable rights. A contract serving the public or benefiting an identifiable group does not automatically give every member a private contract action.

Identify the promisor, promisee, proposed beneficiary, precise performance promised, and evidence of intended enforceability. The beneficiary’s interest must be tied to that contract. Under § 302 a beneficiary is intended only if recognizing a right is appropriate to effectuate the parties' intention and either performance will satisfy the promisee's obligation to pay the beneficiary money (a creditor beneficiary) or the promisee intends to give the beneficiary the benefit (a donee beneficiary); everyone else is incidental and acquires no right (§ 315). The promisor may raise defenses arising from the contract itself against the beneficiary, but not claims from unrelated dealings with the promisee (§ 309; C&M 1196). Questions about vesting and later modification arise only after identifying a right capable of vesting.
